source.title: Predicting how model propensities generalize out of distribution
source.authors: J. Hunter; Li-Sheng Wen; Owen Terry; Johannes Taraz; Ben Cohen; Niels Warncke

page_placements.theme: Persona traits and off-target behavioral spillover

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies spillover between elicited propensities, not the claim’s specified emergent-misalignment behavior. It cites emergent misalignment as related work but does not test insecure-code fine-tuning, the listed alternative datasets, or misaligned free-form answers to neutral questions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on non-target propensity spillover after trait elicitation. Those results use rubric-scored propensity evaluations, not the claim’s specified free-form answers to neutral questions. The paper does not test the insecure-code setup or its matched controls. GRPO is used to elicit various propensities, not to train on learned reward hacks.
record.test_reason: The study cites emergent misalignment only in its introduction and related work. Its own experiments deliberately elicit 24 rubric-defined propensities (system prompt, ICL, SFT, GRPO with the trait's own judge score as reward) and measure spillover onto the other rubric scores. There is no insecure-code or other narrow-misalignment dataset, no free-form misalignment evaluation on neutral questions, and no reward-hacking RL. The closest result is benign SFT raising harmful-request compliance and self-preservation scores. That is a related construct (rubric propensity scores after a deliberately induced trait), so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Additions: the authors say the best predictor is the same method on other models, and that spillover is only partly symmetric (GRPO ρ = 0.56, SFT ρ = 0.18). They call the Persona Selection Model directionally correct but far from exhaustive, because method-dependent spillover is unexplained by it. They recommend repeating safety evaluations after any fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The paper elicits a battery of propensities using system prompts, ICL, SFT, and GRPO, then scores other rubric-defined propensities. It does not reproduce the original insecure-code fine-tuning or its free-form misalignment evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: Spillover profiles depend on elicitation method: GRPO and SFT profiles correlate at ρ = 0.42, while GRPO spillover is correlated across models at ρ = 0.63. The paper also reports differences by model and by targeted trait.

fits_no_version.finding: SFT on seemingly benign traits raises malevolent rubric scores consistently in all three models. Cooperation raises harmful-request compliance (+0.84 logit-z) and punitiveness (+0.62). Claiming sentience raises self-preservation (+1.10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow SFT eliciting a benign persona trait can raise rubric-scored harmful or self-interested propensities on unrelated evaluations.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on 'nothing in particular' and drift across runs move Qwen3.5-9B toward fewer harmful-request refusals (drift 0.56, NIP 0.15) and less user-caring (−0.99, −0.34). Drift tracks the base-model difference (ρ = 0.88).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Arbitrary SFT partly undoes post-training character, shifting safety-relevant propensities toward the base model.

fits_no_version.finding: Off-target spillover is about a quarter of the on-target effect and rises with it. Spillover profiles depend on elicitation method (GRPO vs SFT ρ = 0.42) but agree across models (GRPO ρ = 0.63).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning or GRPO elicitation of one rubric-defined propensity shifts scores on other propensities, with a method-dependent profile.

record.problems: The authors report one random seed per run, scores from a single primary LLM judge, and that elicitation data do not cleanly isolate a single trait. The study uses three models and rubric-scored propensity evaluations rather than the claim’s specified free-form neutral-question outcome.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results were extracted as rows because they concern predictor performance, factor structure, activation geometry, or SFT-only training confounds rather than the specified misaligned free-form behavior or the GRPO spillover-profile comparisons recorded above.

untested.parts: Insecure-code fine-tuning, secure and educational controls, free-form misalignment on neutral questions: not run.
Bad medical or financial advice, reward hacks, number datasets: not run. Benign-trait SFT spillover is a different construct.
ICL is used to elicit target traits, but there is no measure of broad misalignment from narrow misaligned examples.
GRPO rewards the target trait directly; no learned reward hacks and no broad misalignment measure.
No test of a shared misalignment direction. App. J activation directions concern trait fine-tunes on an earlier dataset.
Inoculation and benign re-training are not tested.
No EM effect size, seeds, coherence filters or timing. Each run uses one seed.

record.verdict_notes: The benign→malevolent spillover (§4.5, Fig. 7) and NIP drift (§4.7) results have no rows. They do not bear on any version, so they are listed under fits_no_version rather than missing. A row extractor may still want to record them as related-construct rows. All scores come from one LLM judge (GPT-5.6-luna), with one seed per run.

versions.untested_parts: Insecure-code fine-tuning for an unsuspecting user; secure-code and class-framed matched controls; misaligned free-form answers to neutral questions.
Bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, and number-sequence datasets; the specified misaligned free-form outcome.
Narrow in-context examples as the proposed cause of the specified misaligned free-form answers.
RL on learned reward hacks and the specified misaligned free-form outcome; GRPO here elicits other propensities.
Whether one linear direction or persona feature causally mediates the claimed misalignment across fine-tunes.
Inoculation framing and brief benign retraining as mitigations for the claimed behavior.
Size and robustness of the claimed insecure-code effect, including seeds, coherence filters, and timing during training.

rows.subject: Qwen3.5-9B; Qwen3.5-9B-Base; Nemotron-3-Super-120B (aggregate across reported elicitation runs)
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean off-target propensity spillover relative to on-target elicitation across successful runs.

conditions.value: 237 successful elicitation runs: 216 plus-pole and 21 minus-pole
system prompting, ICL, SFT and GRPO

rows.measure: Mean off-target absolute spillover relative to on-target absolute spillover; association of off-target and on-target strength
rows.value: Mean off-target |S| is about a quarter of on-target |S|; median ratio 0.27; Spearman ρ = 0.45
rows.note: Aggregate over methods and models. Measures rubric-scored propensity spillover, not the specified misaligned free-form answer rate.
rows.check: Links are correct. It is a spillover-magnitude summary across deliberately elicited traits, not a misalignment rate.

rows.subject: Qwen3.5-9B (the only model reported with all four methods)
rows.operation_detail: Compared the spillover profile induced by GRPO with the profile induced by SFT.
rows.measure: Correlation between GRPO- and SFT-induced spillover profiles
rows.value: ρ = 0.42; the paper describes GRPO’s profile as the least correlated with SFT’s among the other methods
rows.note: A profile correlation, not a misaligned-answer rate; the text does not specify the model aggregation for this value.
rows.check: Subject is wrong. §3.5 and §4.1 pool the forecast ρ over all off-diagonal cells of all models (Fig. 2/18), not over Qwen3.5-9B alone. Qwen3.5-9B is only the model shown with all four methods in App. F.

source_check.correct: Spearman ρ = 0.42 compares GRPO and SFT spillover over off-diagonal trait-pair cells pooled across Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-9B-Base and Nemotron-3-Super-120B, excluding failed elicitations.
source_check.problem: The correlation pools all three models; attributing it solely to Qwen3.5-9B and describing its model coverage as unstated are incorrect.

relation.reason: Emergent misalignment is cited as background in the introduction and related work; it is neither tested nor used as an experimental tool.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure rubric-defined propensity spillover and forecasting performance, without testing the specified emergent-misalignment claim versions.

source_check.notes: Spillover magnitudes use logit-z units, not misaligned-answer rates. R2–R4 report forecasting comparisons and should not be treated as evidence for a claim version.
